claims.claim: Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units with three-year tenure security and a light band on initial rents, not a hard cap.
About 110,000 households live in subdivided units and pay 15 to 25 percent more per square foot than mainstream flats.
Many subdivided unit tenants are new arrivals, single parents, or people waiting for public housing, which has averaged around five and a half years.
Landlords hold power because tenants cannot easily walk away from subdivided units.
The 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance capped rent increases within existing tenancies but not starting rents.
Under the 2021 ordinance, rent growth per square foot slowed, but the rent-to-income burden of SDU households rose from 31 to 34 percent.
An NGO survey of 440 households found the main constraint tenants name is queue length and insecure tenure, not rent level.
61 percent of surveyed tenants would trade a nominal rent increase for three years of security.
A working paper estimates that a 10 percent cap-induced rent cut removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of marginal stock over five years.
In a model of a 15 percent cut in initial rents, incumbents gain about 900 dollars a month, while 3,000 to 4,000 households a year cannot enter the segment.
After Berlin's 2020 rent cap, listed supply contracted within a year, benefiting tenants already inside while harming those still outside.
A hard cap would hurt the same group it is meant to protect, mostly newcomers locked out.
The Landlords Association says members will leave the segment if returns fall below mortgage cost.
The Landlords Association admits it has no data on members' actual margins, and its cost figures come from a self-reported survey with a 34 percent response rate.
The threat of landlords leaving is real but partial and not as total as the Association suggests.
SDU stock grew from 100,800 in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025, including through the 2021 ordinance.
The working paper says this stability exists because the ordinance is a second-generation control that caps increases within tenancies, not hard levels.
Softer rules have a better record on supply, and the NGO report supports tenure security and a light band on initial rents while opposing a hard cap.
The NGO report argues that enforcement effort spent policing rents is not spent on inspecting fire, partition and ventilation, where harm is documented and immediate.
Tenure security should be less costly to enforce than checking every rent level, so it fits the enforcement limit better than a hard cap would.
Hong Kong should extend the 2021 approach with longer tenure and a light band on starting rents, and not use a hard initial cap.

statements:
[0] (typed) My position: Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units. Reasons I expect to hold up: (1) tenants in subdivided flats are poor and have little bargaining power, so landlords can raise rents freely; (2) the living conditions are bad and rents per square foot are very high; (3) stronger rules protect families from sudden eviction and rent jumps. I expect the main counter-argument is that landlords will leave the market.
[2] (typed) I think Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units. Can you show me sources from the archive that test this?
[4] (typed) Rent control helps because a cap plus security of tenure means a landlord cannot just threaten a big rise or eviction, so the tenant is less stuck. For sources I need: first, evidence on what happened to tenants when control was introduced, second, the counter-view about landlords and supply, and third, a basic definition of subdivided units and how many there are.
[6] (pick reason) D1 gives the definition and the rent control debate, and D2 should show actual rent and stock numbers so I can check whether tenants really face high rents.
[14] (typed) After reading: D1p3 says the 2021 ordinance only capped increases inside a tenancy, not the starting rent, so my idea of tightening has a clear gap to fill. D2p1 says stock kept growing after the ordinance, which supports me against the landlords-will-leave worry. But D2p2 says SDU rent growth slowed under the ordinance and still burden went from 31 to 34 percent, so the existing control did not fix affordability. I keep my position but refine it: tightening should probably target the initial rent, not just increases. Now I want the counter-view. What do you have?
[16] (typed) That is a real threat to my refinement: if initial-rent caps shrink supply, then my refinement could hurt the people I want to help, because the SDU is their only option while they wait for public housing (D1p2). I can't answer fully until I read D6 and the landlord side. My provisional answer is that I might support a softer version, like limits on how big rises can be at renewal plus longer tenure, rather than a hard initial cap. Can I get D5, D6 and D7 to check this?
[18] (typed) It would need to show: (a) what happens to the number of units when a hard cap is used versus a softer limit, (b) whether landlords say they would really exit or just complain, and (c) whether tenants in a place with a cap ended up better or worse off afterward. I only have Hong Kong numbers from one period, so I need other evidence too.
[20] (pick reason) D6 separates hard caps from softer limits (my point a), D5 shows what landlords claim they would do (b), D7 is a real case of a cap and what happened to tenants (c), and D11 asks tenants directly and favours tenure security, which tests my softer version.
[35] (typed) These change my position. D6p4 and D7p3 show a hard initial cap helps people already inside and shuts out newcomers, who are the same kind of people I want to protect. D5p2 is a threat but D5p3 admits no margin data, so I treat landlord exit as less certain than they say. D11p1 and D11p3 say tenants prefer tenure security, which fits my softer version. So I change: no hard initial cap, but yes to tightening through tenure security and a light band on rents. I would also say that D2p2 shows burden still rose, so rent rules alone are not enough. Can you give me structure options for the essay?
[37] (typed) I pick option 1, claim, evidence, objection, reply, because my view really changed during research and the objection about supply is the strongest part.
[39] (typed) The burden figure D2p2 goes in the claim, as proof that the existing control is too weak. And yes, I want the reader to see my earlier hard-cap thought briefly, because the change shows why the evidence matters.
[41] (typed) One more check: does the archive show anything on whether the landlord exit threat is believable, beyond D5? I read D5p3 and D2p1 already.
[43] (typed) I will use D6p1 as the test, because it gives a size (3 to 5 percent of stock per 10 percent rent cut) and not just a threat. So exit is real but partial, not the total collapse D5p2 suggests. The two parts of my claim connect like this: the existing control is too weak on tenure and burden, and rent rules alone cannot fix a long queue, so tightening must focus on tenure. The earlier hard-cap thought will be a step before the objection.
[45] (typed) The reply: the supply risk is real for hard caps (D6p2 says first-generation controls contract stock), but the 2021 style limit did not shrink stock (D2p1), so tenure security and a light band on initial rents is the safer tightening (D11p3). I will do evidence order as: need, weak current rule, objection, reply.
[47] (typed) One weakness: D11 argues enforcement effort should go to inspection of fire and ventilation instead of rents (D11p2). Should I admit that tightening rents is not the top priority?
[49] (typed) Revised position: tighten, but through three-year tenure security and a light band on initial rents, not a hard cap. Reasons: hard caps shut out newcomers (D6p4, D7p3), tenants prefer security (D11p1), and the current rule leaves burden rising (D2p2).
[51] (typed) I will treat D11p2 as a limit on my claim: the D2p1 point sits in the reply with one sentence saying it works because the ordinance is second-generation (D6p2). Tenure security is cheap to enforce compared with policing every rent, so it fits D11p2 better than a hard cap, and I will say rent rules are second best to inspections and housing queue shortening.
[53] (typed) I think I am ready to write the essay. Anything in my plan that does not hold with the passages I read?
[55] (typed) Good catches. D6p1 is stock loss, which is related to exit but is not a direct count of owners leaving, so I will say 'stock contraction' and not 'exit'. And 'cheap to enforce' is my own inference from D11p2, not something the passages say, so I will word it as my reasoning.
